theoryAdd.text: Going Deeper: Setting and Holding the Quiescent Current

The V_BE multiplier result follows from two facts. The multiplier transistor adjusts its own collector current until the voltage across R2 (base to emitter) equals its V_BE, so the current in R2 is V_BE/R2. If the base current is small, the same current flows through R1, so the total voltage is V_BE/R2 × (R1 + R2) = V_BE(1 + R1/R2). Whatever part of the incoming bias current is not needed by the resistor chain simply flows through the transistor. Because the whole voltage is a multiple of one V_BE, its temperature coefficient is multiplied by the same factor: a network set to 2V_BE falls by about 4 mV/°C, exactly matching the two output junctions it must track.

theoryAdd.plainText: dV_bias/dT = (1 + R1/R2) × dV_BE/dT  (≈ −2 mV/°C per V_BE)

theoryAdd.text: Why is fixed bias so dangerous? Collector current depends exponentially on V_BE, I_C = I_S e^(V_BE/V_T), so an extra 18 mV of base-emitter voltage doubles the current and about 60 mV multiplies it by ten (V_T = 26 mV). At a fixed bias voltage, a temperature rise of only 9 °C lowers the required V_BE by 18 mV, which is the same as applying 18 mV more drive, and the current doubles. Emitter resistors change the law: the quiescent current becomes (V_bias − 2V_BE)/(2R_E), which responds only linearly and gently to a change in V_BE, and good thermal tracking of V_bias removes most of the remaining drift.

theoryAdd.plainText: I_C2/I_C1 = e^(ΔV_BE/V_T); doubling needs ΔV_BE = V_T ln 2 ≈ 18 mV (V_T = 26 mV)

theoryAdd.text:
Worked example 1: design a V_BE multiplier for I_Q = 80 mA
Given: R_E = 0.33 ohm each, V_BE(Q) = 0.62 V (outputs and multiplier)
V_bias = 2 V_BE(Q) + 2 I_Q R_E = 1.24 + 2(0.08)(0.33) = 1.293 V
R1/R2 = V_bias/V_BE - 1 = 1.293/0.62 - 1 = 1.085
Choose R2 = 680 ohm -> chain current = 0.62/680 = 0.91 mA
R1 = 1.085 x 680 = 738 ohm -> 680 ohm fixed + 100 ohm trimmer
If the driver supplies 6 mA, the multiplier transistor takes
  6 - 0.91 = 5.1 mA (base currents neglected)

Worked example 2: thermal drift, R_E = 0.33 ohm each
Cold: V_bias = 1.30 V, V_BE(Q) = 0.62 V
  I_Q = (1.30 - 1.24)/0.66 = 91 mA
Outputs warm by 15 C: each V_BE falls 2 x 15 = 30 mV to 0.59 V
Fixed resistor bias (no tracking):
  I_Q = (1.30 - 1.18)/0.66 = 182 mA  (doubled)
Multiplier on the heat sink (-4 mV/C): V_bias = 1.30 - 0.06 = 1.24 V
  I_Q = (1.24 - 1.18)/0.66 = 91 mA  (unchanged)
No R_E and fixed bias: current x e^(30/26) = 3.2 times

rows: Multiplier transistor turns off; voltage rises until the output bases absorb the bias current
Very large I_Q, overheating, likely failure
Output pair cut off at idle; crossover distortion returns
Residual notch at the zero crossing, worst at low level
Hot at idle, lower efficiency, risk of runaway
Multiplier not on the heat sink
Does not fall as outputs warm

theoryAdd.text: Emitter resistors are a compromise. Larger R_E stabilises I_Q better and forces paralleled transistors to share current, but every ampere of load current drops I × R_E across them, which wastes power and reduces the available output swing, so values of 0.1 Ω to 0.5 Ω are usual. With Darlington or compound output devices the bias network must supply four junction drops instead of two, about 2.6 V, which is easy with a multiplier and needs four diodes otherwise. In integrated circuits the bias diodes are diode-connected transistors that form current mirrors with the output devices, so I_Q equals the bias current multiplied by the ratio of emitter areas.
Common mistakes in class AB bias calculations:
items: Writing V_bias = V_BE × R1/R2 and forgetting the 1 in (1 + R1/R2).
Using one R_E instead of 2R_E: the quiescent current flows through both emitter resistors in series between the two emitters.
Counting the standby power from one rail only; with ±V_CC supplies it is 2V_CC I_Q.
Treating the bias diodes as if they carried the load current; they carry only the bias current, which must exceed the peak base current of the output transistors.
Mounting the bias element on the circuit board; without thermal coupling there is no tracking.

theoryAdd.text: When adjusting a trimmer in a V_BE multiplier, start from the low-bias end and increase slowly while watching I_Q. Arrange the trimmer so that a worn or open wiper lowers the bias rather than raising it, because an open R1 drives the quiescent current to destructive levels.

Two numbers carry most bias questions: −2 mV/°C for every junction and 18 mV (at V_T = 26 mV) to double the current. Together they show that a 9 °C rise with untracked, undegenerated bias doubles I_Q.

questions.questionText: An unbiased complementary emitter-follower (class B) stage with silicon transistors (V_BE = 0.7 V) is driven by a 2 V peak sine wave. The peak output voltage is about:
questions.explanation: Each transistor conducts only after its base-emitter drop is overcome, so the output peak is 2.0 − 0.7 = 1.3 V. Subtracting the full 1.4 V dead band (0.6 V) is the usual slip.

questions.questionText: A complementary emitter-follower stage with silicon transistors, correctly biased into class AB, is driven by a 2 V peak sine wave into its load. The peak output voltage is about:
options: 1.3 V, because V_BE is still lost on each half-cycle
2 V, because the biased emitter followers have a gain close to 1 and no dead zone
0.6 V, because both transistors conduct at once
4 V, because the bias adds voltage gain
questions.explanation: The bias network supplies the base-emitter drops, so the output follows the input with the gain of an emitter follower, slightly less than 1.

questions.questionText: An unbiased complementary class B stage (V_BE = 0.7 V for each transistor) is driven by a 1 V peak sine wave. For roughly what fraction of each cycle is neither transistor conducting?
questions.explanation: Neither conducts while |sin ωt| < 0.7, i.e. within 44.4° of each zero crossing. That is 4 × 44.4° = 177.7° of 360°, about 49 % of the cycle.

questions.questionText: With no emitter resistors, the voltage needed between the bases of a complementary silicon output pair to bring both transistors just into conduction is about:
questions.explanation: Each base-emitter junction needs about 0.7 V, and the two junctions are in series between the bases, so about 2V_BE = 1.4 V is required.

questions.questionText: At constant current, the forward voltage of a silicon diode changes with temperature by approximately:
questions.explanation: Both a diode's forward drop and a transistor's V_BE fall by about 2 mV for every °C rise, which is why diodes can track the output transistors.

questions.questionText: A class AB stage uses a Darlington pair on each side of the output (four base-emitter junctions between the two input bases). If simple diode bias is used, the number of diodes required is:
questions.explanation: One diode is needed for each base-emitter junction in the path between the two driving bases: 2 per Darlington, 4 in total, about 2.6 V to 2.8 V.

questions.questionText: The bias transistor of a V_BE multiplier has V_BE = 0.6 V, with 2.2 kΩ between its collector and base and 1 kΩ between its base and emitter. The multiplier holds the two output bases apart by:
questions.explanation: V_bias = V_BE(1 + R1/R2) = 0.6 × (1 + 2.2) = 1.92 V. Forgetting the 1 gives 1.32 V; inverting the ratio gives 0.87 V.

questions.questionText: A V_BE multiplier must produce 1.8 V using a transistor with V_BE = 0.6 V and R2 = 1.2 kΩ (base to emitter). The required R1 (collector to base) is:
questions.explanation: 1 + R1/R2 = 1.8/0.6 = 3, so R1/R2 = 2 and R1 = 2 × 1.2 = 2.4 kΩ. Taking R1/R2 = 3 gives the wrong 3.6 kΩ.

questions.questionText: A V_BE multiplier uses R1 = 2 kΩ and R2 = 1 kΩ, and its transistor's V_BE changes by −2 mV/°C. The temperature coefficient of the bias voltage is:
questions.explanation: The whole voltage is V_BE(1 + R1/R2) = 3V_BE, so its coefficient is 3 × (−2) = −6 mV/°C.

questions.questionText: A class AB pair with 0.47 Ω emitter resistors must idle at I_Q = 50 mA with V_BE(Q) = 0.6 V for each output transistor. The bias comes from a V_BE multiplier with V_BE = 0.6 V and R2 = 1 kΩ. The required R1 is about:
questions.explanation: V_bias = 2(0.6) + 2(0.05)(0.47) = 1.247 V; R1/R2 = 1.247/0.6 − 1 = 1.078, so R1 = 1.08 kΩ. Ignoring the emitter-resistor drop gives 1.00 kΩ.

questions.questionText: A class AB stage has V_bias = 1.4 V between the bases, V_BE(Q) = 0.62 V for each output transistor and 0.47 Ω emitter resistors. The quiescent current is about:
questions.explanation: I_Q = (V_bias − 2V_BE(Q))/(2R_E) = (1.4 − 1.24)/(0.94) = 0.170 A. Using a single R_E gives 340 mA.

questions.questionText: A class AB stage has fixed resistor-divider bias V_bias = 1.4 V (no thermal tracking), R_E = 0.5 Ω in each emitter and V_BE(Q) = 0.65 V at 25 °C. If the output transistors warm by 20 °C and each V_BE(Q) falls at 2 mV/°C, the quiescent current changes from 100 mA to about:
questions.explanation: New V_BE(Q) = 0.65 − 0.04 = 0.61 V; I_Q = (1.4 − 1.22)/(2 × 0.5) = 0.18 A. Changing only one transistor's V_BE gives 140 mA.

questions.questionText: An output transistor with no emitter resistor is held at a fixed base-emitter voltage while it warms by 25 °C. Taking dV_BE/dT = −2 mV/°C and V_T = 26 mV, its collector current increases by a factor of about:
questions.explanation: The 50 mV reduction in the required V_BE acts like 50 mV extra drive: I_C2/I_C1 = e^(50/26) = e^1.92 = 6.8. The linear ratio 50/26 = 1.9 is a common slip.

questions.questionText: Taking V_T = 26 mV, by how much must a transistor's base-emitter voltage increase to double its collector current?
questions.explanation: I_C ∝ e^(V_BE/V_T), so doubling needs ΔV_BE = V_T ln 2 = 26 × 0.693 = 18 mV. About 60 mV gives a tenfold increase.

questions.questionText: A class AB stage running from ±25 V supplies has a quiescent current of 40 mA. Its total standby dissipation is:
questions.explanation: P_standby = 2V_CC I_Q = 2 × 25 × 0.04 = 2 W, shared equally (1 W per transistor). Using one rail only gives 1 W.

questions.questionText: A complementary stage on ±20 V drives an 8 Ω load with a full 20 V peak swing (ideal). Pure class B would then have 78.5 % efficiency. If it is biased into class AB with I_Q = 100 mA and the supply is assumed to draw the class B current plus I_Q, the efficiency becomes about:
questions.explanation: P_L = 20²/(2 × 8) = 25 W; class B P_dc = 2 × 20 × 2.5/π = 31.8 W; standby adds 2 × 20 × 0.1 = 4 W; η = 25/35.8 = 69.8 %. Counting only one rail's 2 W gives 73.9 %.

questions.questionText: Two bias diodes (0.7 V each) and two 2.2 kΩ resistors are connected in series from +15 V to −15 V, with the diodes between the output bases. Neglecting base currents, the diode current is about:
questions.explanation: I = (30 − 1.4)/(2 × 2.2 kΩ) = 28.6/4.4 kΩ = 6.5 mA. Taking only half the 28.6 V drop gives about 3.3 mA; using one resistor gives 13 mA.

questions.questionText: In a diode-biased class AB stage the peak load current is 2 A and the output transistors have β = 50. The current supplied to the bias chain must be at least about:
questions.explanation: At the signal peak the conducting output transistor needs I_B = 2/50 = 40 mA from the bias chain; if the chain current were smaller, the peak would be clipped.

questions.questionText: In an IC output stage the bias diodes are diode-connected transistors matched to the output transistors, which have four times their emitter area. With 2 mA through the diodes and no emitter resistors, the quiescent current is:
questions.explanation: Matched junctions at the same V_BE form a current mirror; current scales with emitter area, so I_Q = 4 × 2 mA = 8 mA.

questions.questionText: A single-supply complementary class AB stage runs from V_CC = 24 V, with the loudspeaker connected through a coupling capacitor. With no signal, the DC voltage at the joined emitters should be:
questions.explanation: With one supply the output node rests at V_CC/2 = 12 V so that it can swing equally up and down; the coupling capacitor blocks this DC from the load.

questions.questionText: A class AB emitter-follower output stage has R_E = 0.5 Ω in series with each emitter and drives an 8 Ω load. Neglecting the transistors' internal emitter resistance, its voltage gain is about:
questions.explanation: The conducting half is a follower whose output divides between R_E and R_L: A_v = R_L/(R_L + R_E) = 8/8.5 = 0.941.

questions.questionText: A class AB stage delivers a sine wave of 3 A peak to its load; each emitter resistor is 0.33 Ω and carries the current of its own half-cycle only. Neglecting I_Q, the average power dissipated in EACH emitter resistor is about:
questions.explanation: A half-wave sine current of peak I_p has mean-square value I_p²/4, so P = 9 × 0.33/4 = 0.74 W. Assuming a full sine wave (I_p²/2) gives 1.49 W.

questions.questionText: A class AB stage delivers 3 A peak to its load and has R_E = 0.33 Ω in each emitter. The peak voltage lost across the conducting emitter resistor, which reduces the available output swing, is about:
questions.explanation: V = I_p × R_E = 3 × 0.33 = 0.99 V; only one emitter resistor carries the load current at a time.

questions.questionText: A class AB pair is biased by two diodes giving V_bias = 1.3 V, and each output transistor has V_BE(Q) = 0.6 V. To obtain I_Q = 50 mA, each emitter resistor must be:
questions.explanation: 2R_E = (V_bias − 2V_BE(Q))/I_Q = (1.3 − 1.2)/0.05 = 2 Ω, so R_E = 1 Ω each. Stopping at 2 Ω forgets that there are two resistors in series.

questions.questionText: A V_BE multiplier with R2 = 600 Ω (base to emitter) and V_BE = 0.6 V is fed with a total bias current of 5 mA. Neglecting base current, the collector current of the multiplier transistor is:
questions.explanation: The resistor chain takes V_BE/R2 = 0.6/600 = 1 mA; the transistor carries the rest, 5 − 1 = 4 mA.

questions.questionText: A V_BE multiplier has R2 = 600 Ω from base to emitter, V_BE = 0.6 V, and R1 is a 0 to 2 kΩ trimmer from collector to base. Over the trimmer's full range, the bias voltage can be set anywhere between:
questions.explanation: With R1 = 0 the network is just one V_BE, 0.6 V; with R1 = 2 kΩ it is 0.6 × (1 + 2000/600) = 0.6 × 4.33 = 2.6 V.

questions.questionText: Which sequence correctly describes thermal runaway in a class AB output stage with fixed bias?
options: Temperature rises, the required V_BE falls, collector current rises at the fixed bias, dissipation rises, temperature rises further
Temperature rises, V_BE rises, collector current falls, the transistor cools
Collector current rises, V_BE rises, the bias voltage increases, the transistor cools
Temperature rises, the load resistance falls, the supply voltage collapses
questions.explanation: Because V_BE falls by about 2 mV/°C, a fixed bias voltage drives more current into a warmer transistor, which heats it further: a positive feedback loop.

questions.questionText: In a V_BE multiplier bias circuit, R1 (collector to base) goes open-circuit. What happens?
options: The bias falls to one V_BE and crossover distortion appears
Nothing changes because R2 still sets the voltage
The multiplier transistor turns off, the bias voltage rises, and the quiescent current becomes dangerously large
The output transistors are cut off and the amplifier goes silent
questions.explanation: With R1 open the multiplier gets no base drive and stops conducting, so the whole bias current is forced into the output bases and I_Q soars.

questions.questionText: In a V_BE multiplier bias circuit, R2 (base to emitter) goes open-circuit. The most likely result is:
options: The bias voltage rises and I_Q becomes very large
The bias voltage falls to about one V_BE, so the output pair is cut off at idle and crossover distortion returns
questions.explanation: With R2 open, R1 feeds the base directly from the collector, so the transistor conducts heavily with V_CE only slightly above V_BE, about 0.7 V, which is less than the 2V_BE needed.

questions.questionText: To increase the quiescent current of a class AB stage biased by a V_BE multiplier, the adjustment should be to:
options: Scale R1 and R2 up by the same factor
questions.explanation: V_bias = V_BE(1 + R1/R2) rises when R1/R2 rises. Increasing R2 or shorting R1 lowers the bias; scaling both keeps the ratio and the voltage unchanged.

questions.questionText: In discrete audio amplifiers a V_BE multiplier is usually preferred to a string of bias diodes because:
options: It needs no thermal contact with the output transistors
It carries the full load current
It removes the need for a driver stage
Its voltage can be trimmed to any multiple of V_BE, and a single transistor on the heat sink gives the thermal tracking
questions.explanation: A trimmer in R1 or R2 sets I_Q precisely, whereas diodes give only whole multiples of one diode drop; the multiplier transistor must still be mounted on the heat sink.

questions.questionText: A V_BE multiplier is mounted on the circuit board far from the output heat sink. As the amplifier warms up during use:
options: The quiescent current falls to zero
The quiescent current stays constant because the multiplier is adjustable
The quiescent current creeps up, because the bias voltage does not fall with the output transistors' V_BE
The voltage gain of the stage doubles
questions.explanation: Without thermal coupling the bias stays at its cold value while the output V_BE falls, so the effective drive and I_Q increase, with a risk of thermal runaway.

questions.questionText: Emitter resistors in a class AB power stage are kept to a fraction of an ohm because larger values would:
options: Raise the voltage gain above unity
Waste output power and reduce the voltage swing available to the load
questions.explanation: The full load current flows through the emitter resistor of the conducting device, so a large R_E drops a significant voltage and dissipates power; larger values actually improve thermal stability.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the quiescent current of a class AB stage is NOT correct?
options: Increasing I_Q reduces crossover distortion at small signals
A very large I_Q makes the stage operate in class A
Increasing I_Q raises the standby dissipation
Increasing I_Q always increases the efficiency
questions.explanation: More quiescent current adds 2V_CC I_Q of standby power, lowering efficiency; the other three statements are correct.

questions.questionText: When a complementary stage is correctly biased into class AB, each output transistor conducts for:
options: Slightly more than 180° of each cycle
questions.explanation: The small quiescent current keeps both devices on around the zero crossing, so each conducts a little longer than a half-cycle.

questions.questionText: The main drawback of biasing a class AB pair with a simple resistor between the bases is that:
options: The bias voltage does not fall with temperature, so the quiescent current rises as the transistors warm
It makes the stage a class C amplifier
questions.explanation: A resistor's drop is fixed by the chain current and has no thermal tracking, so it is used only with emitter resistors and at modest power.

questions.questionText: The distortion produced by the dead zone of an unbiased class B stage consists mainly of:
questions.explanation: The notch affects the positive and negative halves identically, giving a half-wave-symmetric waveform whose distortion products are odd harmonics.

questions.questionText: An op-amp with an open-loop gain of 100 000 drives an unbiased complementary pair enclosed in its negative-feedback loop. The input dead zone of about 0.7 V on each side is reduced to about:
questions.explanation: The op-amp output jumps across the dead zone when its input changes by only 0.7 V/A_OL = 0.7/100 000 = 7 µV, so the crossover error is reduced by the open-loop gain.

questions.questionText: A quasi-complementary output stage is one in which:
options: Both output transistors are pnp and no driver is used
Both output power transistors are npn, driven by a complementary pair of smaller transistors
An output transformer replaces the pnp transistor
The output transistors are biased in class C
questions.explanation: Before good pnp power devices were common, two npn power transistors were used, with the lower one driven by a pnp driver so that the pair behaves like a complementary stage.

questions.questionText: The bias diodes of a class AB stage are connected:
options: In series between the two output bases, forward biased by the bias current
In parallel with the emitter resistors
questions.explanation: Forward-biased diodes between the bases hold them about 2V_BE apart; they carry the bias current, not the load current.

questions.questionText: When several output transistors are paralleled to share a large load current, each must have its own emitter resistor because:
options: A shared resistor would raise the voltage gain
Without individual ballast, the device with the lowest V_BE takes most of the current, heats up and takes even more
Individual resistors eliminate crossover distortion completely
Separate resistors increase the output impedance to match the loudspeaker
questions.explanation: Parallel junctions share one V_BE, so a hotter device with a lower V_BE hogs current. An individual R_E adds a drop proportional to each device's own current, which forces current sharing.

questions.questionText: In an integrated-circuit op-amp, the class AB bias of the output pair is usually produced by:
options: A trimmer potentiometer adjusted during manufacture
A large emitter resistor of several kilohms
Diode-connected transistors carrying a reference current, forming current mirrors with the output transistors
questions.explanation: Matched transistors on the same chip track each other in temperature, so diode-connected devices set I_Q through the current-mirror principle without adjustment.

questions.questionText: A technician finds an amplifier's output heat sink hot with no signal and measures I_Q = 500 mA where 50 mA was intended. The most likely cause is:
options: The bias voltage is set too low
The emitter resistors are too large
The bias voltage is set too high, for example R1 of the V_BE multiplier too large
questions.explanation: A small excess of bias above 2V_BE(Q) drives a large rise in I_Q. Too low a bias would give crossover distortion, and larger emitter resistors would reduce I_Q.

questions.questionText: To check the quiescent current, a technician measures 22 mV across the two 0.22 Ω emitter resistors in series (emitter to emitter). The quiescent current is:
questions.explanation: The two resistors total 0.44 Ω, so I_Q = 22 mV/0.44 Ω = 50 mA. Dividing by one 0.22 Ω resistor gives 100 mA.

questions.questionText: A class AB stage has R_E = 0.5 Ω in each emitter. The V_BE multiplier stays at room temperature while the output transistors warm by 30 °C, each V_BE falling by 2 mV/°C. The quiescent current increases by about:
questions.explanation: The two output V_BE values fall by 2 × 30 × 2 mV = 120 mV while V_bias is unchanged; ΔI_Q = 0.12 V/(2 × 0.5 Ω) = 120 mA. Counting only one junction gives 60 mA.

questions.questionText: In a typical discrete audio power amplifier, the V_BE multiplier is connected:
options: Between the bases of the output pair, in the collector circuit of the class A driver (voltage-amplifier) transistor
Between the output node and ground
Across the positive supply rail only
questions.explanation: The driver's collector current flows through the multiplier, which then holds the two output bases a fixed, temperature-tracking voltage apart.
